A discrete complement of Lyapunov’s inequality and its information theoretic consequences

James Melbourne and Gerardo Palafox-Castillo
Abstract.

We establish a reversal of Lyapunov’s inequality for monotone log-concave sequences, settling a conjecture of Havrilla-Tkocz and Melbourne-Tkocz. A strengthened version of the same conjecture is disproved through counter example. We also derive several information theoretic inequalities as consequences. In particular sharp bounds are derived for the varentropy, Rényi entropies, and the concentration of information of monotone log-concave random variables. Moreover, the majorization approach utilized in the proof of the main theorem, is applied to derive analogous information theoretic results in the symmetric setting, where the Lyapunov reversal is known to fail.

1. Introduction

In this paper we prove the following reversal of Lyapunov’s inequality11 1 By Lyapunov’s inequality we refer to the fact that p↦log⁡‖f‖ppp\mapsto\log\|f\|_{p}^{p} is convex in pp for a general measurable function ff and measure., conjectured in [33] and [18].

Theorem 1.1.

For xx, a monotone, log-concave sequence in ℓ1\ell_{1}, the function

t↦log⁡(t​∑ixit)\displaystyle t\mapsto\log\left(t\sum_{i}x_{i}^{t}\right)

is strictly concave for t∈(0,∞)t\in(0,\infty).

This is anticipated by affirmative results in the continuous setting dating back to Cohn [10] on ℝ\mathbb{R}, and Borell [9] in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. However in contrast to the continuous setting, the requirement that xx is monotone cannot be dropped22 2 Note that for continuous variables on ℝ\mathbb{R}, proving the result for monotone variables is equivalent to the general result since log-concavity is preserved under rearrangement, see for example [31]., see [33] for examples. Moreover, we will also provide a counter example to a strengthening of Theorem 1.1 conjectured in [33, 18], further differentiating the continuous and discrete settings.

The main novelty in the proof is to establish a majorization between the distribution function of a monotone log-concave sequence and its geometric counterpart. Though we will not expound upon this outside of its application to this proof, it can be understood as a second order analog of the distributional majorization lemma utilized in [34, 32]. This alongside some further reductions, leaves one needing only the special case of a geometric sequence, which can be approached with direct computation, to complete the proof of Theorem 1.1.

This effort fits within a more general pursuit, developing discrete analogs for the continuous convexity theory, which in recent investigation has connected information theory and convex geometry (see [25] for background). One instantiation is the effort to understand the behavior of the entropy of discrete variables under independent summation, see [19, 27, 33, 24, 7]. Another is the pursuit of discrete Brunn-Minkowski type inequalities [15, 35, 30, 20, 16, 14, 40, 17]. In fact, in information theoretic language, the Brunn-Minkowski inequality can be understood as a “Rényi entropy power” inequality, see [5, 22, 8, 29, 26, 21, 38, 37], and in this sense, as an information theoretic inequality as well.

We will see that Theorem 1.1 yields several information theoretic consequences for discrete monotone variables. We obtain sharp bounds on the varentropy to be compared to its continuous analog [13], and utilize this to derive concentration of information, analogous to [2, 13]. We give sharp reversals of the monotonicity of Rényi entropy general parameters, augmenting the recently obtained comparisons for the ∞\infty-Rényi entropy given in [33], and as a consequence we obtain a sharp reverse entropy power type inequality for iid variables, tightening a result from [33]. We mention that this reverse entropy power is the discrete analog of an entropic Rogers-Shephard inequality pursued by Madiman and Kontoyannis in [23]. We also obtain a sharp comparison between the value of a log-concave sequence at its mean, and the value at its mode which we compare with the classical result of Darroch [12] for Bernoulli sums. We will also obtain as a Corollary of our arguments that for the monotone log-concave variables of a fixed pp-Rényi entropy, the geometric distribution has maximal qq-Rényi entropy for q≥pq\geq p and minimal qq-Rényi entropy for q≤pq\leq p.

As mentioned, Theorem 1.1 can fail without the assumption of monotonicity. In particular, symmetric variables do not necessarily satisfy the conclusion of Theorem 1.1. However we will demonstrate that the majorization techniques used are robust enough to be applied in the symmetric case, and we use them to deliver sharp Rényi entropy comparisons, varentropy bounds, and concentration of information results in the symmetric setting. We also establish the “symmetric geometric” distribution as the maximal (resp. minimal) qq-Rényi entropy distribution for fixed pp-Rényi entropy among discrete symmetric log-concave variables for q≥pq\geq p (resp. q≤pq\leq p).

Let us outline the paper. In Section 2, we will define notation and derive applications of the main theorem. In Section 3 we give the proof of Theorem 1.1. In Section 4 we give a counter example to the strengthening of Theorem 1.1 conjectured in [18, 33], while in Section 5, we derive analogs of the consequences in Section 2 for symmetric log-concave variables. In the Appendix A we recall some elementary results from the theory of majorization for the convenience of the reader.

2. Applications

2.1. Definitions

For a real valued random variable YY, we let 𝔼​Y\mathbb{E}Y denote its expectation, and denote its variance Var⁡(Y)≔𝔼​Y2−(𝔼​Y)2{\rm Var}(Y)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}Y^{2}-(\mathbb{E}Y)^{2}.

Definition 2.1.

Let (E,μ)(E,\mu) be a measure space and XX an EE valued random variable with density function ff such that ℙ⁡(X∈A)=∫Af​𝑑μ\mathbb{P}(X\in A)=\int_{A}fd\mu. We define the information content IX:E→ℝI_{X}:E\to\mathbb{R}, as IX​(x)=−log⁡f⁡(x)I_{X}(x)=-\log f(x).

To avoid confusion, in sections where we discuss the information content random variable IX​(X)I_{X}(X), we will avoid the usual abuse of notation and write H⁡(f)H(f) for the entropy of a variable XX. Conversely, when there is no risk of confusion, and we are considering a single variable XX, we will omit the subscript and write II for the information content. We write H(μ)​(X)=H(μ)​(f)≔𝔼​I​(X)H_{(\mu)}(X)=H_{(\mu)}(f)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}I(X) in the general case. For example, when EE is discrete, and μ\mu is the counting measure,

𝔼​I​(X)=H⁡(X)\mathbb{E}I(X)=H(X)

is just the Shannon entropy of XX. Observe that when μ\mu is a probability measure given by a random variable YY, then the expectation of the information content is given by the relative entropy (or Kullbeck-Leibler divergence), H(μ)(f)=−D(X||Y)H_{(\mu)}(f)=-D(X||Y), and the varentropy measures the deviation of −I⁡(X)-I(X) from D(X||Y)D(X||Y).

In physical applications, it may be more natural to write the density of XX in terms of a potential EE, f⁡(x)=e−E⁡(x)f(x)=e^{-E(x)}, in which case, 𝔼​I​(X)\mathbb{E}I(X) reflects the average energy of a system, and V⁡(X)V(X) the average fluctuation.

Definition 2.2.

For a random variable XX taking values on a measure space (E,μ)(E,\mu) with density function ff, define the varentropy functional,

(1) V⁡(X)=𝔼​(log⁡f⁡(X)−𝔼​log⁡f⁡(X))2.\displaystyle V(X)=\mathbb{E}(\log f(X)-\mathbb{E}\log f(X))^{2}.

Unless specified, we will consider E=ℤE=\mathbb{Z} and μ\mu the standard counting measure, so that the density function xn≔ℙ⁡(X=n)x_{n}\coloneqq\mathbb{P}(X=n) of a variable XX, can be expressed as a non-negative sequence.

Definition 2.3.

A non-negative sequence xix_{i} is log-concave when

xi2≥xi−1​xi+1x_{i}^{2}\geq x_{i-1}x_{i+1}

and i≤j≤ki\leq j\leq k with xi​xk>0x_{i}x_{k}>0 implies xj>0x_{j}>0.

We consider a sequence to be increasing when xi​xi+1>0x_{i}x_{i+1}>0 implies xi+1≥xix_{i+1}\geq x_{i}, and decreasing when xi​xi+1>0x_{i}x_{i+1}>0 implies xi+1≤xix_{i+1}\leq x_{i}. A sequence is monotone when it is either increasing or decreasing.

Definition 2.4.

A random variable XX taking values in ℤ\mathbb{Z} is log-concave when the sequence xi≔ℙ⁡(X=i)x_{i}\coloneqq\mathbb{P}(X=i) is log-concave. The variable XX is monotone when the sequence xix_{i} is monotone.

We say a non-negative sequence xix_{i} belongs to ℓp\ell_{p} when ∑i∈ℤxip<∞\sum_{i\in\mathbb{Z}}x_{i}^{p}<\infty. Note that when xix_{i} is log-concave, xix_{i} belonging to ℓ1\ell_{1} implies that xix_{i} belongs to ℓp\ell_{p} for all p∈(0,∞)p\in(0,\infty).

The following result is actually a consequence of the Rényi entropy comparison derived in [33]. It does not need the assumption of monotonicity. The result should be compared to the classical result of Darroch [12], that states that for independent sums of Bernoulli random variables the distance between the mean and mode is no greater than 1, see also [36, 41, 24] for background and recent developments on such variables. For the larger class of log-concave variables such a result is impossible. For example, a geometric distribution has mode at 00, but can have arbitrarily large expectation. However, the result below demonstrates that the value of any log-concave distribution at its mean approximates up to an absolute constant ee, the value of the distribution at its mode.

Corollary 2.8.

For XX with log-concave density function ff with support A⊆ℤA\subseteq\mathbb{Z},

max⁡{f⁡(⌊𝔼​X⌋),f⁡(⌈𝔼​X⌉)}≥e−1​‖f‖∞\displaystyle\max\{f(\lfloor\mathbb{E}X\rfloor),f(\lceil\mathbb{E}X\rceil)\}\geq e^{-1}\ \|f\|_{\infty}

where ⌊⋅⌋\lfloor\cdot\rfloor and ⌈⋅⌉\lceil\cdot\rceil denote the usual floor and ceiling.

Note that inequality is sharp in the sense that the constant e−1e^{-1} cannot be improved, as can be seen by choosing a geometric distribution with large, integer valued mean.

Define the log-affine interpolation of ff,

Then log⁡f~\log\tilde{f} is a concave function on c​o​(A)co(A) the convex hull of AA, and by Jensen’s inequality and

H⁡(f)=−𝔼​log⁡f⁡(X)=−𝔼​log⁡f~​(X)≥−log⁡f~​(𝔼​X).\displaystyle H(f)=-\mathbb{E}\log f(X)=-\mathbb{E}\log\tilde{f}(X)\geq-\log\tilde{f}(\mathbb{E}X).

Using that by Theorem 2.7 and by Theorem 1.3 of [33] in the absence of monotonicity, H⁡(f)≤H∞​(f)+1H(f)\leq H_{\infty}(f)+1, and inserting the inequality into exponentials we have

exp⁡(−log⁡‖f‖∞+1)\displaystyle\exp(-\log\|f\|_{\infty}+1) ≥exp⁡(−log⁡f~​(𝔼​X))\displaystyle\geq\exp(-\log\tilde{f}(\mathbb{E}X))
e‖f‖∞\displaystyle\frac{e}{\|f\|_{\infty}} ≥1f~​(𝔼​X)\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{\tilde{f}(\mathbb{E}X)}

which yields

e​max⁡{f⁡(⌊𝔼​X⌋),f⁡(⌈𝔼​X⌉)}≥f1−(𝔼​X−⌊𝔼​X⌋)​(⌊𝔼​X⌋)​f𝔼​X−⌊𝔼​X⌋​(⌈𝔼​X⌉)≥‖f‖∞\displaystyle e\max\{f(\lfloor\mathbb{E}X\rfloor),f(\lceil\mathbb{E}X\rceil)\}\geq f^{1-(\mathbb{E}X-\lfloor\mathbb{E}X\rfloor)}(\lfloor\mathbb{E}X\rfloor)f^{\mathbb{E}X-\lfloor\mathbb{E}X\rfloor}(\lceil\mathbb{E}X\rceil)\geq\|f\|_{\infty}

2.5. Renyi Entropy Power Reversals

The entropy power inequality, is a fundamental inequality in information theory that gives a sharp lower bound on the amount of entropy increase in summation of continuous independent variables, explicitly taking μ\mu to be the Lebesgue measure on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and denoting for XX with density ff with respect to μ\mu N⁡(X)=e2d​H(μ)​(f)N(X)=e^{\frac{2}{d}H_{(\mu)}(f)}, Shannon’s entropy power inequality states that N⁡(X+Y)≥N⁡(X)+N⁡(Y)N(X+Y)\geq N(X)+N(Y) for independent random vectors XX and YY. More generally, super-additivity properties of the Rényi entropy have been studied, extending the Shannon’s EPI, see [4, 37, 25, 21, 22, 29, 38]. We consider a Rényi Entropy Power reversal to be any non-trivial upper bound on the entropy of a sum of random variables, see [3, 6, 11, 43, 1, 42, 7].

Theorem 2.11.

For X,YX,Y iid, log-concave, and monotone on ℤ\mathbb{Z}, and α∈[2,∞]\alpha\in[2,\infty]

Hα​(X−Y)≤Hα​(X)+log⁡2.\displaystyle H_{\alpha}(X-Y)\leq H_{\alpha}(X)+\log 2.

The inequality is a sharp improvement for monotone log-concave variables of Theorem 6.2 of [33], where it is proven that Hα​(X−Y)≤Hα​(X)+α1α−1​log⁡2H_{\alpha}(X-Y)\leq H_{\alpha}(X)+\alpha^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}}\log 2 for XX and YY iid and log-concave. To see that the constant 22 cannot be improved, take XX to have density f⁡(n)=(1−p)​pnf(n)=(1-p)p^{n} so that for n≥0n\geq 0, fX−Y​(n)=1−p1+p​p|n|f_{X-Y}(n)=\frac{1-p}{1+p}p^{|n|}. Taking the limit with p→1p\to 1 shows the inequality to be sharp. An alternative motivation for the inequality is its relationship to an entropic generalization conjectured by Madiman and Kontoyannis [23] of the Rogers-Shephard inequality from convex geometry [39], see also [33] for further discussion.

The proof relies on an elementary trick, known to specialists, that H2​(X)=H∞​(X−Y)H_{2}(X)=H_{\infty}(X-Y) holds for iid variables XX and YY. We include a proof for completeness and emphasize that this equality is independent of any property of the distribution44 4 The proof is given for iid log-concave XX and YY in [33]..

Lemma 2.12.

For XX and YY iid on ℤ\mathbb{Z},

(6) H2​(X)=H∞​(X−Y).\displaystyle H_{2}(X)=H_{\infty}(X-Y).
Proof.

Let ff denote the shared distribution of XX and YY and fX−Yf_{X-Y} the distribution of X−YX-Y. We compute directly,

Proposition 3.3.

Let XX be a random variable on the non-negative integers and the sequence xi≔ℙ⁡(X=i)x_{i}\coloneqq\mathbb{P}(X=i), then for t≥1t\geq 1, Fx​(λ)F_{x}(\lambda) as defined in Proposition 3.2 satisfies

If U,VU,V are non-negative random variables with densities f,gf,g respectively, such that 𝔼⁡(U)=𝔼⁡(V)\mathbb{E}(U)=\mathbb{E}(V), and f≤gf\leq g on an interval II, and f≥gf\geq g outside II, then

A natural generalization of Theorem 1 was first conjectured in an early version of [18], and reiterated in [33].

A random variable on ℤ\mathbb{Z} can be symmetric about a point m∈ℤm\in\mathbb{Z} (f⁡(m+n)=f⁡(m−n)f(m+n)=f(m-n)) or it could be symmetric about n+12n+\frac{1}{2} for n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}. For example ℙ⁡(X=0)=ℙ⁡(X=1)=12\mathbb{P}(X=0)=\mathbb{P}(X=1)=\frac{1}{2} is symmetric about 0+120+\frac{1}{2}. In this case, when a log-concave sequence (xi)i∈ℤ(x_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{Z}} is symmetric about a point n+12n+\frac{1}{2},

log⁡(t​∑ixit)=log⁡(t​∑i>nxit)+log⁡2\displaystyle\log\left(t\sum_{i}x_{i}^{t}\right)=\log\left(t\sum_{i>n}x_{i}^{t}\right)+\log 2

Clearly S⁡(0)=1S(0)=1. while limλ→1(1−λ)p1−λp=0\lim_{\lambda\to 1}\frac{(1-\lambda)^{p}}{1-\lambda^{p}}=0. By the intermediate value theorem, since SS is continuous for λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1), there must be a λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1) such that S⁡(λ)=∑zip=∑ixipS(\lambda)=\sum z_{i}^{p}=\sum_{i}x_{i}^{p}.

A similar approach will handle the case that p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1). ∎

Proposition 5.5.

If xix_{i} is non-increasing for i≥0i\geq 0 and zz is symmetric geometric, then there exists a finite interval II such that

(19) Fx​(t)≥Fz​(t)\displaystyle F_{x}(t)\geq F_{z}(t) t∈I\displaystyle\quad t\in I
(20) Fx​(t)≤Fz​(t)\displaystyle F_{x}(t)\leq F_{z}(t) t∉I\displaystyle\quad t\notin I
Proof.

We know the result to be true for x∗=(xi)i≥0x^{*}=(x_{i})_{i\geq 0} and z∗=(zi)i≥0z^{*}=(z_{i})_{i\geq 0} by Proposition 3.2. Now, see that

2​Fx∗−1=Fx,2F_{x^{*}}-1=F_{x},

and

2​Fz∗−1=Fz.2F_{z^{*}}-1=F_{z}.

Furthermore, Fx≥FzF_{x}\geq F_{z} if and only if 2​Fx∗−1≥2​Fz∗−12F_{x^{*}}-1\geq 2F_{z^{*}}-1 if and only if Fx∗≥Fz∗F_{x^{*}}\geq F_{z^{*}}. Similarly for Fx≤FzF_{x}\leq F_{z}. Therefore the same interval II given by Proposition 3.2 satisfies our desired inequalities. ∎

Lemma 5.6.

Let XX be log-concave, symmetric about a point n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}. Then there exists a symmetric geometric distribution ZZ, such that Hp​(X)=Hp​(Z)H_{p}(X)=H_{p}(Z) and

Hq​(X)≥Hq​(Z)\displaystyle H_{q}(X)\geq H_{q}(Z)

for q≥p>0q\geq p>0, and

Hq​(X)≤Hq​(Z),\displaystyle H_{q}(X)\leq H_{q}(Z),

for 0<q≤p0<q\leq p.

Proof.

First, see that Hp​(X)=Hp​(Z)H_{p}(X)=H_{p}(Z) if and only if ∑ixip=∑izip\sum_{i}x_{i}^{p}=\sum_{i}z_{i}^{p} so there must exist such geometric distribution for p≠1p\neq 1 by Proposition 5.4. Suppose Hp​(X)=Hp​(Z)H_{p}(X)=H_{p}(Z). Let UU be a random variable with density FzF_{z}, and VV be a random variable with density FxF_{x}. Since ∑xip=∑zip\sum x_{i}^{p}=\sum z_{i}^{p} then 1p​∑xip=1p​∑zip\frac{1}{p}\sum x_{i}^{p}=\frac{1}{p}\sum z_{i}^{p}, which implies 𝔼⁡(Vp−1)=𝔼⁡(Up−1)\mathbb{E}\left(V^{p-1}\right)=\mathbb{E}\left(U^{p-1}\right) by Proposition 3.3. Let g⁡(x)=xq−1p−1g(x)=x^{\frac{q-1}{p-1}}. If p>1p>1 and q∈(1,p)q\in(1,p), we have that g⁡(x)g(x) is concave, thus 𝔼⁡(g⁡(Vp−1))≥𝔼⁡(g⁡(Up−1))\mathbb{E}\left(g(V^{p-1})\right)\geq\mathbb{E}\left(g(U^{p-1})\right) by Proposition 3.2 and Theorem 3.5.Thus 𝔼⁡(Vq−1)≥𝔼⁡(Uq−1)\mathbb{E}\left(V^{q-1}\right)\geq\mathbb{E}\left(U^{q-1}\right) and, multiplying both sides by qq and using Proposition 3.3, we get ∑xiq≥∑ziq\sum x_{i}^{q}\geq\sum z_{i}^{q}. The same can be argued if p<1p<1 and q∈(p,1)q\in(p,1). Now, when p>1p>1 and q∈(0,1)∪[p,∞)q\in(0,1)\cup[p,\infty), and when p<1p<1 and q∈(0,p]∪(1,∞)q\in(0,p]\cup(1,\infty), g⁡(x)g(x) is convex, so by Theorem 3.5 the inequality is reversed and ∑xiq≤∑ziq\sum x_{i}^{q}\leq\sum z_{i}^{q}. Now, to pass from the sum to Rényi’s entropy, we must multiply by 11−q\frac{1}{1-q}, which reverses the inequality when q>1q>1. So we get

1<q<p\displaystyle 1<q<p ⇒Hq​(X)≤Hq​(Z);\displaystyle\Rightarrow H_{q}(X)\leq H_{q}(Z);
q<1<p\displaystyle q<1<p ⇒Hq​(X)≤Hq​(Z);\displaystyle\Rightarrow H_{q}(X)\leq H_{q}(Z);
q<p<1\displaystyle q<p<1 ⇒Hq​(X)≤Hq​(Z);\displaystyle\Rightarrow H_{q}(X)\leq H_{q}(Z);
1<p<q\displaystyle 1<p<q ⇒Hq​(X)≥Hq​(Z);\displaystyle\Rightarrow H_{q}(X)\geq H_{q}(Z);
p<1<q\displaystyle p<1<q ⇒Hq​(X)≥Hq​(Z);\displaystyle\Rightarrow H_{q}(X)\geq H_{q}(Z);
p<q<1\displaystyle p<q<1 ⇒Hq​(X)≥Hq​(Z).\displaystyle\Rightarrow H_{q}(X)\geq H_{q}(Z).

The limiting cases with qq or p∈{1,∞}p\in\{1,\infty\} can be easily handled using continuity and monotonicity of the Rényi entropy as a function of α↦Hα​(X)\alpha\mapsto H_{\alpha}(X) and as a function of the parameter λ\lambda of a symmetric geometric distribution ZλZ_{\lambda}, λ→Hα​(Zλ)\lambda\to H_{\alpha}(Z_{\lambda}). ∎

Theorem 5.7.

For XX log-concave and symmetric about a point n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}, p≥qp\geq q, then

∎

Appendix A Majorization

The following theorem is a well known characterization of the convex order, see [28] for proof and further background.

Theorem A.1.

For XX and YY are random variables on [0,∞)[0,\infty) such that 𝔼​X=𝔼​Y<∞\mathbb{E}X=\mathbb{E}Y<\infty, then

(21) 𝔼​φ​(Y)≥𝔼​φ​(X)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\varphi(Y)\geq\mathbb{E}\varphi(X)

holds for all convex functions φ\varphi, if it holds for all φ\varphi of the form φ⁡(x)=[x−t]+\varphi(x)=[x-t]_{+} for t∈(0,∞)t\in(0,\infty).

When XX and YY satisfy (21) we say that YY majorizes XX in the convex order, or just that YY majorizes XX for short, and write Y≻XY\succ X.

Theorem A.2.

For non-negative random variables X∼fX\sim f and Y∼gY\sim g with densities taking values on [0,∞)[0,\infty) such that 𝔼​X=𝔼​Y<∞\mathbb{E}X=\mathbb{E}Y<\infty, if there exists an interval I⊆[0,∞)I\subseteq[0,\infty) such that g≤fg\leq f on II, and g≥fg\geq f on [0,∞)−I[0,\infty)-I, then Y≻XY\succ X.

Proof.

For t∈[0,∞)t\in[0,\infty) define Ψ⁡(t)=𝔼​[Y−t]+−𝔼​[X−t]+\Psi(t)=\mathbb{E}[Y-t]_{+}-\mathbb{E}[X-t]_{+}. By assumption 𝔼​X=𝔼​Y\mathbb{E}X=\mathbb{E}Y, and hence Ψ⁡(0)=0\Psi(0)=0. By monotone convergence, limt→∞Ψ⁡(t)=0\lim_{t\to\infty}\Psi(t)=0. Computing the derivatives of Ψ\Psi, one obtains Ψ′​(t)=ℙ⁡(X>t)−ℙ⁡(Y>t)\Psi^{\prime}(t)=\mathbb{P}(X>t)-\mathbb{P}(Y>t), and Ψ′′​(t)=g⁡(t)−f⁡(t)\Psi^{\prime\prime}(t)=g(t)-f(t). Observe that Ψ′​(0)=0\Psi^{\prime}(0)=0, limt→∞Ψ′​(t)=0\lim_{t\to\infty}\Psi^{\prime}(t)=0, and 0=𝔼​Y−𝔼​X=∫0∞Ψ′​(t)​𝑑t0=\mathbb{E}Y-\mathbb{E}X=\int_{0}^{\infty}\Psi^{\prime}(t)dt. Thus, Φ′\Phi^{\prime} must be both positive and negative or it is exactly 00 and the problem is trivial. As such Φ′′\Phi^{\prime\prime} is positve, negative, and then positive. It follows that Φ′\Phi^{\prime} is positive and then negative, and hence Φ≥0\Phi\geq 0 and our result follows. ∎
